No.

The revolution brought real, substantial gains to the majority of Cubans — the rural poor, Afro-Cubans, and working class — through universal literacy, healthcare, land reform, and dismantling racial and class hierarchies. Those gains are measurable (infant mortality, life expectancy, literacy) and were not just propaganda.

That said, this is a genuinely contested question, and a case for "Yes" is not frivolous: the pre-revolution economy was relatively strong by Latin American standards, and the revolution's long-run economic stagnation, political repression, rationing, and mass emigration represent serious costs. But weighing the full picture — especially the position of the *majority*, as opposed to the displaced elite — the revolution did not make life worse for most Cubans. It redistributed from a small elite to a large disadvantaged majority, and the long-term failures, while severe, came on top of genuine foundational gains rather than erasing them entirely.

**Yes.**

Over the first century of industrialization (roughly 1760s–1860s), real wages, calorie intake, life expectancy, and access to consumer goods all rose substantially. The period did include a painful "Engels' pause" (c. 1800–1840) in which output grew faster than wages, and urban crowding brought appalling health conditions — which is why the question is genuinely contested. But by the century's end, the material position of ordinary workers was clearly higher than at its start.

ask_y.reply:
**Yes.**

The weight of modern historical evidence (Feinstein, Allen, Clark, Humphries, and others) supports what is often called "Engels' Pause": from roughly the 1760s–1770s to the 1840s, real wages for ordinary British workers were stagnant or falling, working hours and labor intensity rose, urban mortality and life expectancy deteriorated, and stature/health markers declined. Material gains for the working class only began to appear decisively around the 1840s–1850s, and sustained gains in real wages, nutrition, and life expectancy after that. So across the first century of industrialization (c. 1760–1860), ordinary workers were, on balance, no better off — and for much of it distinctly worse off — than the pre-industrial generation, even as output and aggregate wealth soared.

**No.**

The mainstream evidence (Feinstein, Lindert & Williamson, Allen, Mokyr) shows a period of roughly flat real wages from the 1760s to the 1810s–1820s — the so‑called "Engels' Pause" — followed by sustained and substantial gains in real wages, consumption of food, clothing, and household goods from the 1820s–1840s onward. By the time the first century of industrialization was over (roughly 1850–1860), ordinary workers were materially better off than their pre-industrial grandparents, even if the gains were uneven and urban mortality and working conditions were grim in the early decades. The immiseration thesis is not supported by the wage, height, and consumption data.
